questions.b: It associates the input with a <form id="orderForm"> located anywhere in the document, even if placed outside the <form> tags
questions.c: It converts the input into a subform
questions.d: It links a CSS stylesheet to the form
questions.explanation: The 'form' attribute allows inputs placed outside of <form> container tags to be explicitly attached to that form.

questions.question: What is the 'formaction' attribute on a <button type="submit"> used for?
questions.a: It specifies a CSS animation on submit
questions.b: It overrides the parent form's 'action' URL specifically when that button is used to submit the form
questions.c: It converts the form to a GET request
questions.d: It validates form fields with JavaScript
questions.explanation: 'formaction' overrides the default form action endpoint for the specific submit button clicked.

questions.question: What does 'formmethod' attribute on a submit button do?
questions.b: It overrides the parent form's HTTP method (GET/POST) specifically for this submission button
questions.explanation: 'formmethod="post"' overrides the form's default method when clicked.

questions.question: What does the 'formnovalidate' attribute on a submit button do?
questions.a: It submits the form without triggering client-side browser validation
questions.explanation: 'formnovalidate' on a submit button (such as a 'Save Draft' button) submits data without enforcing client-side validation rules.

questions.question: Which event fires on a form when a user submits it in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The 'submit' event is dispatched to the form element upon submission, allowing event.preventDefault() to intercept it.

questions.question: Which input type creates a single-line text field?
questions.explanation: <input type="text"> is the default form control for single-line text entry.

questions.question: Which input type visually masks the characters entered by the user (usually replacing them with dots or asterisks)?
questions.explanation: <input type="password"> obscures the entered text for basic visual security.

questions.question: How do you group radio buttons so that selecting one automatically deselects the others?
questions.a: Give them all the same 'id' attribute
questions.b: Give them all the same 'class' attribute
questions.c: Give them all the same 'name' attribute
questions.explanation: Radio buttons (<input type="radio">) are mutually exclusive when they share the exact same 'name' attribute.

questions.question: Which input type allows the user to select ZERO or MORE options from a predefined list?
questions.explanation: Checkboxes allow users to select multiple options independent of one another.

questions.question: Which element creates a drop-down selection menu?
questions.explanation: The <select> element is used to create a drop-down list. It contains <option> tags representing available choices.

questions.question: What is the difference between <input type="text"> and <textarea>?
questions.a: <textarea> allows multiple lines of text input; type="text" is single-line
questions.b: <textarea> is used for code; type="text" is for regular writing
questions.c: type="text" has no character limit; <textarea> is limited to 255 characters
questions.explanation: The <textarea> tag defines a multi-line text input control, often used for comments or messages.

questions.question: Why might a developer choose the <button> tag over <input type="button">?
questions.b: <button> elements can wrap content like text, images, or icons; <input> cannot
questions.explanation: Because

questions.question: Which input type provides a native graphical color picker on supported browsers?
questions.explanation: <input type="color"> provides a native UI for selecting a color, submitting the value as a hex code (e.g., #ff0000).

questions.question: Which tag allows you to group related <option> elements within a <select> drop-down menu, creating a non-clickable header?
questions.explanation: The <optgroup> element groups related options in a drop-down list, labeled by its 'label' attribute.

questions.question: What does the <datalist> element do when connected to an <input>?
questions.a: It forces the user to pick only from a predefined list (like a standard select)
questions.b: It connects the input to an external database
questions.c: It provides a dropdown of autocomplete suggestions while still allowing custom typing
questions.d: It formats the input data into a table upon submission
questions.explanation: <datalist> provides an 'autocomplete' feature for <input> elements. Users see a drop-down of suggestions but can still type their own value.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type provides a native slider control?
questions.explanation: <input type="range"> displays a slider control. It uses 'min' and 'max' attributes to define the range of numbers.

questions.question: Which tag is used to draw a visual box around related form elements and group them together?
questions.explanation: The <fieldset> element groups related data in a form and typically draws a box around them. It is often used with <legend>.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type provides a specialized control for entering email addresses and validates format automatically?
questions.explanation: <input type="email"> provides built-in email pattern validation and shows an '@' symbol on mobile virtual keyboards.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type is optimized for entering website URLs?
questions.explanation: <input type="url"> ensures input begins with a valid protocol scheme (e.g. http://) and optimizes mobile keyboards.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type is designed for entering telephone numbers?
questions.explanation: <input type="tel"> brings up a numeric telephone keypad on mobile devices.

questions.question: Which input type restricts user entry to numerical numbers and provides increment/decrement spinner arrows?
questions.explanation: <input type="number"> enforces numerical input and supports min, max, and step attributes.

questions.question: Which input type displays a native date picker (year, month, day)?
questions.explanation: <input type="date"> provides a native graphical calendar date picker in supported browsers.

questions.question: Which input type allows the user to select a time (hours, minutes)?
questions.explanation: <input type="time"> provides a native interface for entering time values.

questions.question: Which input type provides a combined calendar date and time picker with local timezone?
questions.explanation: <input type="datetime-local"> provides a combined date and time selector without timezone offset.

questions.question: Which input type creates a file selector dialog allowing users to upload one or more files?
questions.explanation: <input type="file"> allows users to choose files from their local storage device for upload.

questions.question: Which attribute on <input type="file"> allows the user to select multiple files simultaneously?
questions.explanation: The 'multiple' boolean attribute permits selecting more than one file in file upload dialogs.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the allowed file extensions or MIME types on an <input type="file"> (e.g. '.pdf,image/*')?
questions.explanation: The 'accept' attribute restricts file selection dialogs to specified file extensions or MIME types.

questions.question: Which input type creates a hidden field that stores data not visible to the user, but submitted with the form?
questions.explanation: <input type="hidden"> embeds background parameters (like user IDs, CSRF tokens, session keys) in form submissions.

questions.question: Which input type creates a clickable graphical image button that submits the form and sends click coordinates?
questions.explanation: <input type="image" src="submit.png"> behaves like a submit button while transmitting mouse click coordinates.

questions.question: Which input type is specifically designed for search query inputs, often adding a clear ('X') button?
questions.explanation: <input type="search"> formats search fields and provides native clear buttons in many browsers.

questions.question: How do you pre-select a checkbox or radio button so it appears checked on page load?
questions.explanation: The 'checked' boolean attribute sets the initial state of a checkbox or radio button to selected.

questions.question: How do you pre-select an <option> inside a <select> drop-down menu on page load?
questions.explanation: The 'selected' attribute designates the initially chosen <option> inside a <select> menu.

questions.question: Which attributes control the default visible dimensions of a <textarea> multiline text box?
questions.explanation: <textarea rows="4" cols="50"> specifies the default visible height in text rows and width in character columns.

questions.question: What does the 'multiple' attribute on a <select> element do?
questions.b: Converts the dropdown into a scrollable list box allowing multiple option selections
questions.c: Duplicates the select menu across all forms
questions.explanation: The 'multiple' attribute turns a <select> dropdown into a multi-select list box.

questions.question: Which element represents the completion progress of a task as a progress bar in HTML5?
questions.explanation: <progress value="70" max="100"> renders a native progress bar indicating task progression.

questions.question: Which attribute prevents a form from being submitted if the input field is left empty?
questions.explanation: The 'required' boolean attribute specifies that an input field must be filled out before submitting the form.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'placeholder' attribute?
questions.a: It sets the default value that gets submitted with the form
questions.b: It provides a short hint that is displayed in the input field before the user enters a value
questions.c: It reserves physical space for the input box on the screen
questions.d: It hides the input text for passwords
questions.explanation: The 'placeholder' attribute displays a temporary, greyed-out hint inside the input field that disappears once the user starts typing.

questions.question: What is the critical difference between the 'readonly' and 'disabled' attributes?
questions.a: Readonly fields are sent when the form submits; disabled fields are not sent
questions.b: Disabled fields can be focused by clicking; readonly fields cannot
questions.c: Readonly applies only to textareas; disabled applies to all inputs
questions.d: There is no difference in how the browser handles them
questions.explanation: A 'readonly' field cannot be modified but its value is still submitted. A 'disabled' field is unusable, unclickable, and its value is ignored upon submission.

questions.question: Which attribute limits the maximum number of characters a user can enter into a text input?
questions.explanation: The 'maxlength' attribute enforces a strict character limit on an input or textarea.

questions.question: What does the 'size' attribute control on an <input type="text">?
questions.a: The maximum number of characters allowed
questions.b: The visible width of the input field, measured in characters
questions.c: The font size of the typed text
questions.d: The maximum file size for an upload field
questions.explanation: The 'size' attribute specifies the visible width of an input element, typically in average character widths.

questions.question: Which attribute allows you to enforce a specific Regular Expression (Regex) that the input value must match?
questions.explanation: The 'pattern' attribute allows developers to define a regular expression the input's value is checked against on form submission.

questions.question: Which attributes are used together to specify the allowed numerical range for an <input type="number">?
questions.explanation: The 'min' and 'max' attributes specify the minimum and maximum allowed values for numerical and date inputs.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the legal number intervals for an input field (e.g., only allowing multiples of 5)?
questions.explanation: The 'step' attribute dictates the legal number intervals (e.g., step="5" allows 0, 5, 10, 15).

questions.question: Which attribute automatically places the cursor inside a specific input field when the page loads?
questions.explanation: The 'autofocus' boolean attribute directs the browser to automatically focus that input control when the page finishes loading.

questions.question: How do you disable the browser's automatic suggestion drop-down for a specific input field?
questions.explanation: Setting autocomplete="off" prevents the browser from offering historical suggestions or saved credentials for that specific field.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the <meter> element in HTML5?
questions.b: Representing a scalar measurement within a known range, or a fractional value (such as disk usage, temperature, or battery level)
questions.c: Creating progress bars for file downloads
questions.explanation: <meter> represents a gauge value within a known range (with min, max, low, high, optimum attributes).

questions.question: What is the difference between <progress> and <meter> elements?
questions.a: <progress> is for tasks in progress (e.g. upload %); <meter> is for static gauge measurements within a range (e.g. disk space)
questions.explanation: <progress> represents progress towards completion; <meter> measures a quantity within fixed limits.

questions.question: Which attribute sets the minimum allowed numerical value on <input type="number"> or date inputs?
questions.explanation: The 'min' attribute sets the lower bound value allowed in numerical and date inputs.

questions.question: Which attribute sets the maximum allowed numerical or date value?
questions.explanation: The 'max' attribute sets the upper bound value for inputs.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the legal stepping interval for numerical values (e.g. step="0.01" for currency)?
questions.explanation: The 'step' attribute controls the granularity and step increments (or 'any' for floating points).

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the minimum number of characters required in a text field for valid submission?
questions.explanation: 'minlength' enforces a minimum character length constraint before submission.

questions.question: Which attribute on an <input> specifies a Regular Expression (Regex) pattern the value must match to pass validation?
questions.explanation: The 'pattern' attribute (e.g. pattern="[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{4}") verifies text against a regex pattern.

questions.question: How is the 'title' attribute used when a 'pattern' attribute validation fails?
questions.a: It logs an error in console
questions.b: The browser displays the title text as a helpful error tooltip describing the required pattern format to the user
questions.d: It translates the error to Latin
questions.explanation: When pattern validation fails, the browser includes the 'title' text in the validation error message bubble.

questions.question: What does the 'inputmode' attribute do on mobile devices (e.g. inputmode="numeric")?
questions.b: Selects which virtual soft keyboard layout (e.g. numeric, decimal, tel, email) to display without changing the input type
questions.explanation: 'inputmode' (e.g. inputmode="decimal") hints to mobile browsers which on-screen keyboard to present.

questions.question: What is the 'enterkeyhint' attribute used for on mobile inputs?
questions.b: Customizes the label/icon on the virtual keyboard's Enter key (e.g. 'send', 'next', 'search', 'done')
questions.c: Plays an audio click on Enter
questions.explanation: 'enterkeyhint' customizes the text or action icon displayed on the mobile keyboard's Enter key.

questions.question: What is the CSS pseudo-class used to style an input when its current value fails HTML5 constraint validation?
questions.explanation: The ':invalid' CSS pseudo-class matches any form control that currently fails validation constraints.

questions.question: What is the CSS pseudo-class used to style an input that meets all its HTML5 validation constraints?
questions.explanation: The ':valid' CSS pseudo-class styles form controls that satisfy all active validation constraints.

questions.question: What is the CSS pseudo-class used to target an input that possesses the 'required' attribute?
questions.explanation: ':required' targets elements with the required attribute, while ':optional' matches non-required fields.

questions.question: What does the 'checkValidity()' DOM method do when called on an HTML form or input element in JavaScript?
questions.b: Checks if the element satisfies its constraints and returns true if valid or false if invalid (firing an 'invalid' event)
questions.explanation: 'checkValidity()' evaluates constraints and returns true/false without displaying browser error popups.

questions.question: What does 'reportValidity()' do when called on an input element?
questions.b: Checks validity and immediately displays the native browser error validation bubble if the element is invalid
questions.c: Sends an error email to the admin
questions.explanation: 'reportValidity()' evaluates validity and natively displays the constraint validation popup if invalid.

questions.question: How do you set a custom validation error message on an input element in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: 'input.setCustomValidity("message")' sets a custom validation error (passing an empty string clears it).

questions.question: What does the <output> element represent in an HTML form?
questions.b: The result of a calculation or user action (e.g., calculated mortgage payment from sliders)
questions.c: The raw JSON response from the server
questions.explanation: The <output> element semantically represents calculated output derived from user inputs in a form.

questions.question: What attribute connects an <output> element to the inputs used in its calculation?
questions.explanation: <output for="num1 num2"> uses the 'for' attribute to list the IDs of the inputs that contribute to the calculation.

questions.question: What happens to data in an input with the 'disabled' attribute during form submission?
questions.a: It is submitted with value null
questions.b: It is excluded completely from the submitted form data payload
questions.explanation: Disabled form controls are omitted from the form submission dataset entirely (unlike readonly inputs, which are submitted).

questions.question: What happens to data in an input with the 'readonly' attribute during form submission?
questions.a: It is omitted from form data
questions.b: It cannot be edited by the user, but its value IS submitted with the form data
questions.c: It turns into a hidden input
questions.explanation: A 'readonly' field prevents user editing while still including its value in the submitted form payload.

questions.question: Which tag is used to display a completely separate web page within the current HTML document?
questions.explanation: The <iframe> (inline frame) is used to embed another document (like a YouTube video or external site) within the current HTML document.

questions.question: Which iframe attribute applies extra security restrictions on the content embedded within it?
questions.explanation: The 'sandbox' attribute enables an extra set of restrictions for the content in the iframe, such as blocking script execution or form submission.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the <script> tag?
questions.b: To embed or reference executable client-side code, typically JavaScript
questions.c: To display code snippets safely on the screen
questions.explanation: The <script> tag is used to embed client-side scripts (JavaScript) or point to an external script file using the 'src' attribute.

questions.question: What does the <noscript> element do?
questions.a: It instructs the browser to block all ads on the page
questions.b: It disables JavaScript for the entire document
questions.c: It provides alternative HTML content for users whose browsers do not support JavaScript or have it disabled
questions.d: It minifies JavaScript code before execution
questions.explanation: Content inside <noscript> is only rendered if the user's browser has JavaScript disabled or does not support client-side scripting.

questions.question: Which attribute on a <script> tag ensures that the external script is executed only after the HTML document has been completely parsed?
questions.explanation: The 'defer' attribute tells the browser to continue parsing the HTML and execute the script only after the DOM is fully built.

questions.question: Which tag was traditionally used to embed plug-ins like Flash or Java Applets, but is now rarely used?
questions.explanation: The <object> tag was heavily used to embed multimedia plug-ins. While still valid, HTML5's native video/audio elements have largely replaced it.

questions.question: When embedding an external script, which attribute is used to provide the file path?
questions.explanation: Just like an image, external scripts use the 'src' attribute (e.g., <script src="app.js"></script>).

questions.question: How is the <embed> tag different from <object> and <iframe>?
questions.a: It does not require a closing tag
questions.d: It only works for audio files
questions.explanation: The <embed> tag is an empty (void) element and therefore has no closing tag, unlike <object> and <iframe>.

questions.question: What does the <iframe> element stand for and do?
questions.b: Inline Frame: it embeds another independent HTML document inside the current webpage
questions.c: Internal Frame: it creates CSS Grid borders
questions.d: Interface Frame: it runs native desktop applications
questions.explanation: <iframe> (Inline Frame) embeds a nested browsing context containing another HTML page inside the current document.

questions.question: Which attribute specifies the source document URL on an <iframe>?
questions.explanation: The 'src' attribute specifies the address URL of the embedded document.

questions.question: What does the 'sandbox' attribute do on an <iframe> when specified with no flags (<iframe sandbox>)?
questions.b: Applies maximum security restrictions (disables scripts, form submissions, popups, and same-origin access)
questions.c: Enables full access to webcam and microphone
questions.d: Translates the iframe into a sandbox game
questions.explanation: An empty 'sandbox' attribute enforces maximum sandbox restrictions on the iframe content.

questions.question: Which sandbox token allows an iframe to execute JavaScript?
questions.explanation: sandbox="allow-scripts" re-enables JavaScript execution within the sandboxed iframe.

questions.question: Which sandbox token allows a sandboxed iframe to submit forms?
questions.explanation: sandbox="allow-forms" permits form submissions from inside the iframe.

questions.question: Which sandbox token allows a sandboxed iframe to open popups or new windows (e.g. target="_blank")?
questions.explanation: sandbox="allow-popups" allows the iframe to spawn new browser tabs/windows.

questions.question: Which attribute allows an iframe to request full-screen mode (e.g. for embedded YouTube videos)?
questions.explanation: The 'allowfullscreen' boolean attribute enables the iframe to invoke the Fullscreen API.

questions.question: What is the 'allow' attribute (Permissions Policy) used for on <iframe> elements?
questions.b: Explicitly granting or restricting access to browser features and APIs (like camera, microphone, geolocation, payment)
questions.explanation: The 'allow' attribute defines Permissions Policy directives (e.g. allow="camera; microphone; geolocation").

questions.question: What does the 'srcdoc' attribute do on an <iframe>?
questions.b: Specifies the raw HTML content of the page to embed directly inline, overriding 'src'
questions.c: Generates automatic documentation for the iframe
questions.explanation: 'srcdoc' provides inline HTML markup rendered inside the iframe rather than loading an external URL.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'async' attribute on a <script> tag?
questions.b: Downloads the script asynchronously in the background while parsing HTML, and executes it immediately as soon as download completes
questions.c: Runs the script on a Web Worker thread
questions.explanation: <script async> fetches the script without blocking HTML parsing, executing it immediately upon download completion.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'defer' attribute on a <script> tag?
questions.a: Cancels script execution if an error occurs
questions.b: Downloads the script in the background during HTML parsing and executes it in order only AFTER the HTML document has been completely parsed
questions.c: Defers script execution until user clicks
questions.explanation: <script defer> downloads asynchronously and guarantees execution in document order after the DOM is fully constructed.

questions.question: What is the difference in execution order between multiple 'async' vs multiple 'defer' scripts?
questions.a: 'defer' scripts execute in exact document order; 'async' scripts execute in whatever order they finish downloading
questions.c: There is no difference in order
questions.explanation: Defer preserves script execution order; async executes each script as soon as it arrives, potentially out of order.

questions.question: What does 'type="module"' on a <script> tag do in modern browsers?
questions.a: Loads the script as an ES6 JavaScript module (enabling import/export syntax, deferred execution by default, and strict mode)
questions.explanation: <script type="module"> enables standard ES6 module imports, automatic strict mode, and deferred execution.

questions.question: What is the <noscript> tag used for in HTML?
questions.b: It displays fallback content to users who have disabled JavaScript or whose browser does not support scripting
questions.explanation: <noscript> content renders only when client-side scripting is disabled or unsupported.

questions.question: What is the <object> element used for in HTML?
questions.b: Embedding external multimedia, PDF documents, ActiveX controls, or interactive browser plugins
questions.explanation: <object data="file.pdf" type="application/pdf"> embeds external objects and multimedia with nested fallback content.

questions.question: Which tag is used inside <object> or <applet> to pass name/value configuration parameters to an embedded plugin?
questions.explanation: <param name="autoplay" value="true"> passes parameter configuration to <object> plugins.

questions.question: What is the <embed> element in HTML5?
questions.a: A self-closing void container for embedding external applications or multimedia plugins (like PDF readers)
questions.b: A tag that embeds CSS styles
questions.c: A tool for embedding SQL queries
questions.explanation: <embed> is a void element that acts as an integration point for external non-HTML applications or media.

questions.question: What is the HTTP response header 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' used for by web servers?
questions.b: Preventing other websites from embedding this page in an <iframe>, protecting against Clickjacking attacks
questions.explanation: X-Frame-Options: DENY prevents the page from being framed by any domain, thwarting clickjacking exploits.

questions.question: Which Content Security Policy (CSP) directive is the modern replacement for X-Frame-Options?
questions.explanation: CSP's 'frame-ancestors' directive specifies valid parent domains that may embed the webpage.

questions.question: What does 'loading="lazy"' do when added to an <iframe> in modern browsers?
questions.a: Loads the iframe only on double click
questions.b: Defers fetching and loading the iframe document until the user scrolls near the iframe viewport
questions.d: Mutes all audio inside the iframe
questions.explanation: loading="lazy" on an iframe delays loading offscreen embedded documents until scrolled near.

questions.question: What is Subresource Integrity (SRI) on a <script> tag (e.g. integrity="sha384-...")?
questions.a: A check that enforces HTTPS encryption
questions.b: A security feature that verifies the cryptographic hash of an externally hosted script (like a CDN) to prevent compromised scripts from executing
questions.d: A tool to verify CSS syntax
questions.explanation: The 'integrity' attribute ensures third-party CDN scripts have not been tampered with or compromised.

questions.question: What does the 'nomodule' attribute on a <script> tag do in modern browsers?
questions.a: Prevents the script from executing in browsers that support ES6 modules (serving as fallback for legacy browsers)
questions.d: Runs the script without strict mode
questions.explanation: 'nomodule' ensures legacy fallback scripts are ignored by modern browsers that understand ES6 modules.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed sound files into a web page natively?
questions.explanation: The <audio> tag is the native HTML5 standard for embedding sound files.

questions.question: Which attribute must be added to <audio> or <video> tags to display play, pause, and volume buttons?
questions.explanation: Adding the boolean 'controls' attribute instructs the browser to display its native playback interface.

questions.question: Why is the <source> tag used inside <video> and <audio> elements?
questions.a: To allow the browser to choose from multiple file formats depending on its compatibility
questions.b: To apply external CSS styling to the media player
questions.c: To fetch the media file faster
questions.d: To define the copyright metadata of the media
questions.explanation: Providing multiple <source> tags (e.g., MP4 and WebM) ensures fallback support; the browser will play the first format it understands.

questions.question: Modern browsers block videos from playing automatically. How do you bypass this restriction using HTML attributes?
questions.c: Autoplay cannot be bypassed with HTML; it requires JavaScript
questions.explanation: Due to user experience policies, browsers block autoplaying media with sound. Adding the 'muted' attribute allows 'autoplay' to function silently.

questions.question: Which attribute on the <video> tag specifies an image to be shown while the video is downloading or until the user hits play?
questions.explanation: The 'poster' attribute takes a URL for an image to display before video playback begins.

questions.question: Which element is used to attach timed text tracks, such as subtitles or captions, to a <video>?
questions.explanation: The <track> element is placed inside <video> or <audio> to specify subtitles, caption files, or other text tracks.

questions.question: What does the 'loop' attribute do on a media element?
questions.a: It loops a specific 5-second section of the video
questions.b: It automatically restarts the media file from the beginning once it reaches the end
questions.c: It plays all media files on the page in a continuous sequence
questions.d: It reverses the playback once it finishes
questions.explanation: The boolean 'loop' attribute causes the audio or video to start over automatically every time it finishes.

questions.question: What is the correct way to handle browsers that do not support the <audio> element at all?
questions.a: There is no fallback; the page will crash
questions.b: Place fallback text directly between the <audio> and </audio> tags
questions.c: Use the 'fallback' attribute on the audio tag
questions.d: Redirect them to a different webpage automatically
questions.explanation: Any text placed between the opening and closing <audio> or <video> tags is displayed only if the browser doesn't recognize the element.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed video content natively into a webpage without external plugins?
questions.explanation: The <video> element provides native multimedia playback for video streams and files.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is used to embed audio streams and sound files natively?
questions.explanation: The <audio> element provides native audio playback without requiring third-party plugins.

questions.question: What does the 'controls' attribute do on a <video> or <audio> element?
questions.b: Displays native browser playback controls (play/pause button, seek timeline, volume bar, fullscreen toggle)
questions.c: Locks media playback with a password
questions.d: Connects the media to a remote server
questions.explanation: The 'controls' attribute reveals the browser's built-in player controls interface.

questions.question: What does the 'autoplay' attribute do on an <audio> or <video> element?
questions.b: Instructs the browser to start playing the media automatically as soon as it is ready
questions.c: Downloads all videos on the website
questions.explanation: 'autoplay' initiates playback automatically as soon as sufficient data has buffered.

questions.question: Why do modern browsers block video 'autoplay' unless the 'muted' attribute is also present?
questions.a: To prevent bandwidth loss on slow modems
questions.b: To prevent disruptive unsolicited noise from alarming users when browsing webpages
questions.c: Because audio cannot be decoded with video
questions.d: To comply with copyright DRM laws
questions.explanation: Browsers enforce autoplay policies preventing unmuted audio from playing without prior user interaction.

questions.question: What does the 'loop' attribute do on a media element?
questions.b: Automatically restarts playback from the beginning when it reaches the end
questions.explanation: 'loop' causes the audio or video to continuously restart once it finishes playing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'poster' attribute on a <video> tag?
questions.a: Specifies a banner ad to display over the video
questions.b: Specifies an image thumbnail URL to display before the video starts playing or while downloading
questions.c: Prints a poster of the video frame
questions.explanation: The 'poster' attribute specifies a placeholder image displayed until the video is played.

questions.question: What does the 'preload' attribute configure on a media element?
questions.b: Hints to the browser how much media data to buffer in advance ('none', 'metadata', or 'auto')
questions.explanation: 'preload' advises the browser whether to fetch 'none', 'metadata' (duration/dimensions), or 'auto' (the entire file).

questions.question: What is the purpose of nested <source> elements inside <video> or <audio>?
questions.a: To play multiple videos simultaneously in split-screen
questions.b: To specify alternative media file formats (e.g., MP4, WebM, OGG) so the browser can select the first format it supports
questions.explanation: Multiple <source src="..." type="..."> tags provide format fallbacks for cross-browser codec compatibility.

questions.question: Which element is used to add subtitles, captions, or chapter descriptions to a <video> or <audio> element?
questions.explanation: <track> links timed text tracks (subtitles, captions, descriptions) to media elements.

questions.question: What standard file format is used for timed text tracks linked via the <track> element in HTML5?
questions.explanation: WebVTT (.vtt) is the standard format for HTML5 media subtitles and captions.

questions.question: What 'kind' attribute value on a <track> element is used for subtitles translated into a different language?
questions.explanation: kind="subtitles" provides translation of dialogue when the viewer does not understand the language.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'captions' and 'subtitles' in the <track> element?
questions.a: 'captions' include dialogue plus sound effects and audio descriptions for the deaf/hard-of-hearing; 'subtitles' only translate spoken dialogue
questions.explanation: Captions provide full acoustic transcription (dialogue + sound cues) for accessibility; subtitles only transcribe dialogue.

questions.question: Which attribute sets a <track> element as the active enabled track by default?
questions.explanation: The 'default' boolean attribute enables the specified track unless user preferences override it.

questions.question: What does the 'srclang' attribute specify on a <track> element (e.g. srclang="en")?
questions.a: The programming language of the parser
questions.b: The natural language of the text track data
questions.explanation: srclang specifies the BCP 47 language code of the text track content.

questions.question: Which attribute allows an iOS/Safari video element to play inline inside the webpage instead of forcing automatic fullscreen?
questions.explanation: The 'playsinline' attribute allows video playback within the page layout on iOS devices without taking over the full screen.

questions.question: What does 'disablePictureInPicture' attribute do on a <video> element?
questions.b: Prevents the browser from offering Picture-in-Picture mode popout window for this video
questions.explanation: 'disablePictureInPicture' removes the Picture-in-Picture context option in supported browsers.

questions.question: What does 'controlsList="nodownload"' do on an HTML5 video player?
questions.b: Hints to the browser's native media player to hide the download button from the controls menu
questions.c: Encrypts the video stream with DRM
questions.explanation: 'controlsList="nodownload"' instructs the native media UI to suppress the download button in supported browsers.

questions.question: Which JavaScript method begins playback of an <audio> or <video> element?
questions.explanation: 'media.play()' returns a Promise that initiates media playback.

questions.question: Which JavaScript method pauses an active <audio> or <video> playback?
questions.explanation: 'media.pause()' halts playback at the current timestamp.

questions.question: Which DOM property reports or sets the current playback position of a media element in seconds?
questions.explanation: 'media.currentTime' accesses or changes the playback position in seconds.

questions.question: What is the Media Source Extensions (MSE) API in HTML5 used for?
questions.a: Playing MP3 files from hard drives
questions.b: Allowing JavaScript to generate media streams dynamically and feed chunks of video into HTML5 <video> elements (enabling adaptive streaming like HLS/DASH)
questions.explanation: MSE enables adaptive bitrate streaming protocols (HLS/DASH) by allowing JavaScript to buffer media segments into video elements.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTML5 <canvas> and <svg>?
questions.a: Canvas is vector-based; SVG is raster/pixel-based
questions.b: Canvas draws graphics on the fly using JavaScript pixels; SVG defines vector graphics using XML tags
questions.c: Canvas is only for 3D; SVG is only for 2D
questions.d: Canvas is deprecated; SVG is the modern standard
questions.explanation: Canvas is a pixel-based raster drawing API manipulated via JavaScript. SVG is a resolution-independent vector format written in XML.

questions.question: Can you draw a rectangle inside a <canvas> element using only HTML tags?
questions.b: No, <canvas> acts only as a container; all drawing must be done via JavaScript
questions.d: No, rectangles require external image files
questions.explanation: The <canvas> tag itself is completely blank. Developers must use JavaScript (e.g., getContext('2d')) to actually draw shapes and pixels.

questions.question: Which tag creates a circle when placed inside an <svg> element?
questions.explanation: SVG uses straightforward XML tags like <circle>, <rect>, and <polygon> to render vector shapes directly in the DOM.

questions.question: Which HTML5 API allows a web application to find the user's physical longitude and latitude (if the user grants permission)?
questions.explanation: The HTML Geolocation API (accessed via navigator.geolocation in JS) is used to locate a user's position.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'localStorage' and 'sessionStorage' in HTML Web Storage?
questions.a: localStorage is secure; sessionStorage is not
questions.b: localStorage stores data with no expiration date; sessionStorage data is deleted when the browser tab is closed
questions.d: localStorage is for text; sessionStorage is for media
questions.explanation: sessionStorage is temporary and scoped to the specific browser tab. localStorage persists indefinitely until explicitly cleared.

questions.question: What is the purpose of HTML5 Web Workers?
questions.a: To scrape data from other websites
questions.b: To run JavaScript scripts in the background without affecting the performance of the UI/page
questions.c: To automatically update the HTML DOM
questions.d: To handle form validations on the server side
questions.explanation: Web Workers allow intense JavaScript execution on a separate thread, keeping the main web page responsive.

questions.question: How do you make a standard HTML element capable of being dragged by the user using the native HTML Drag and Drop API?
questions.explanation: Adding draggable="true" tells the browser that the user is allowed to click and drag the element.

questions.question: What does SSE stand for in the context of HTML5 APIs?
questions.explanation: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is an API that allows a web page to get automated, one-way updates from a server (like stock tickers or news feeds).

questions.question: When working with <canvas> in JS, what does canvas.getContext('2d') return?
questions.c: A drawing context object that provides methods and properties for drawing shapes and images
questions.d: The pixel width and height of the canvas
questions.explanation: getContext('2d') returns the built-in HTML5 object that holds the actual drawing methods (like fillRect, strokeText).

questions.question: Which of the following data types can Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage) natively store?
questions.explanation: The Web Storage API can only store string key/value pairs. To store objects, developers must use JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse().

questions.question: What does SVG stand for in web development?
questions.explanation: SVG stands for Scalable Vector Graphics, an XML-based vector image format standard.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of SVG vector graphics over raster images (PNG, JPEG)?
questions.b: SVGs scale infinitely to any resolution or zoom level without pixelation or quality loss, and their elements can be styled with CSS
questions.c: SVGs load faster on dial-up modems
questions.d: SVGs cannot be indexed by search engines
questions.explanation: SVGs are mathematical vector shapes that retain pristine clarity at any display density and integrate with CSS/DOM.

questions.question: Which SVG element is used to draw a straight line between two coordinate points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2)?
questions.explanation: <line x1="0" y1="0" x2="100" y2="100" stroke="black" /> draws a straight line in SVG.

questions.question: Which SVG element is used to draw a rectangle or square?
questions.explanation: <rect x="10" y="10" width="50" height="50" /> defines a rectangle.

questions.question: Which SVG element is used to define complex custom vector paths and curves using path data commands (d="M ...")?
questions.explanation: <path d="M150 0 L75 200 L225 200 Z" /> defines complex lines, arcs, and bezier curves.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTML5 <canvas> and <svg> rendering?
questions.a: <canvas> is pixel-based raster rendering via JavaScript; <svg> is DOM-node vector-based retained-mode graphics
questions.b: <svg> is rendered in 3D only; <canvas> is 2D only
questions.c: <canvas> can be styled with CSS classes, whereas <svg> cannot
questions.d: <canvas> elements are saved as PDF files automatically
questions.explanation: Canvas is an immediate-mode bitmap surface driven by JS commands; SVG maintains individual DOM elements for each shape.

questions.question: How do you specify the drawing context dimensions of a <canvas> correctly?
questions.a: Using CSS width and height only
questions.b: Using the HTML 'width' and 'height' attributes directly on the <canvas> element to set the coordinate buffer resolution
questions.d: Canvas dimensions are always fixed at 300x150 and cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Setting width/height on the <canvas> tag sets its internal bitmap buffer resolution; CSS width/height scales the surface.

questions.question: What method on the Geolocation API retrieves the device's current geographic location once?
questions.explanation: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() requests current latitude and longitude coordinates.

questions.question: What method on the Geolocation API continuously monitors location changes as the user moves?
questions.explanation: watchPosition() registers a handler function that is called automatically each time device location updates.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between 'localStorage' and 'sessionStorage' in Web Storage API?
questions.b: localStorage persists indefinitely until cleared; sessionStorage is wiped as soon as the browser tab or session ends
questions.c: sessionStorage stores data on the backend server
questions.explanation: localStorage persists across browser restarts; sessionStorage data is deleted when the browser tab closes.

questions.question: What is the typical storage capacity limit for localStorage per origin in modern browsers?
questions.explanation: Web Storage (localStorage / sessionStorage) typically provides around 5MB–10MB of key-value storage per domain origin.

questions.question: Which method stores a key-value pair in localStorage?
questions.explanation: localStorage.setItem(key, value) saves strings into localStorage.

questions.question: Which method retrieves a stored item from localStorage?
questions.explanation: localStorage.getItem(key) retrieves the string value associated with the specified key.

questions.question: What is IndexedDB in HTML5 web applications?
questions.a: A relational SQL database running in PHP
questions.b: A low-level, high-capacity client-side NoSQL transactional database for storing large amounts of structured data, objects, and blobs
questions.c: A cloud database managed by Google
questions.explanation: IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional client-side NoSQL object store supporting gigabytes of complex structured data.

questions.question: What is the purpose of HTML5 Web Workers?
questions.b: Running JavaScript scripts in background threads independent of the main UI thread, preventing long computations from freezing the UI
questions.explanation: Web Workers execute heavy JS logic on background worker threads without blocking main UI rendering or user interactions.

questions.question: Can a Web Worker directly access or manipulate the DOM (e.g. document.getElementById)?
questions.b: No, Web Workers cannot access the DOM, window, or document objects directly; they communicate with the main thread via postMessage()
questions.c: Only if granted permission in manifest.json
questions.explanation: Workers have no DOM access for thread safety; they exchange data via structured cloning through postMessage() and onmessage.

questions.question: What is a Service Worker in modern Progressive Web Apps (PWAs)?
questions.a: A server daemon running on Apache
questions.b: A specialized programmable client-side proxy that intercepts network requests, manages offline caching, and receives push notifications
questions.d: A tool that compresses HTML files
questions.explanation: Service Workers act as client-side network proxies, enabling offline capabilities, custom cache strategies, and push notifications.

questions.question: What does the WebSocket API (new WebSocket('ws://...')) enable in HTML5?
questions.b: Full-duplex, persistent two-way communication channels over a single TCP connection between browser and server
questions.explanation: WebSockets provide real-time, low-latency, bidirectional persistent communication between client and server.

questions.question: Which HTML5 API allows web applications to detect if the user's device has an active internet connection?
questions.explanation: navigator.onLine returns boolean connectivity status, complemented by 'online' and 'offline' window events.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Notification API (new Notification('Title')) in HTML5?
questions.b: Displaying system-level desktop or mobile push notifications to the user outside the webpage viewport (after user permission is granted)
questions.explanation: The Notification API delivers native operating system desktop and mobile notification banners to users.

questions.question: What does 'WCAG' stand for in web development?
questions.explanation: WCAG is the international standard outlining how to make web content more accessible to people with disabilities.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes?
questions.b: To provide extra information and context to screen readers and assistive technologies
questions.c: To ensure forms are submitted securely
questions.explanation: ARIA attributes (like role="alert" or aria-hidden="true") act as an overlay to provide context missing from native HTML to assistive tech.

questions.question: What happens when you add aria-hidden="true" to an HTML element?
questions.a: It hides the element visually via CSS
questions.b: It hides the element entirely from screen readers, while leaving it visually visible
questions.c: It encrypts the text content inside the tag
questions.d: It prevents the user from highlighting the text
questions.explanation: aria-hidden="true" instructs screen readers to skip the element, which is useful for purely decorative icons or duplicate visual information.

questions.question: Which attribute allows you to make a non-interactive element (like a <div>) focusable using the keyboard's Tab key?
questions.explanation: Setting tabindex="0" inserts an element into the logical keyboard navigation flow, making it focusable.

questions.question: What is the HTML Character Entity used to display a 'less than' symbol (<) without the browser interpreting it as the start of a tag?
questions.explanation: The entity '<' stands for 'less than'. Using actual < signs in text can break HTML parsing.

questions.question: What does the character entity ' ' represent?
questions.explanation: A Non-Breaking Space ( ) creates a space between words that prevents the browser from breaking them apart onto separate lines.

questions.question: Why is URL Encoding necessary when sending data over the web?
questions.b: To ensure the server recognizes the doctype
questions.c: Because URLs can only be sent over the internet using the ASCII character set
questions.explanation: URLs must use the ASCII character set. Unsafe characters (like spaces) must be encoded (e.g., a space becomes %20 or +).

questions.question: What organization actively maintains the 'Living Standard' of HTML today?
questions.c: WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group)
questions.explanation: The WHATWG maintains the HTML Living Standard, having taken over primary governance from the W3C.

questions.question: When validating HTML code, what does the W3C Markup Validation Service primarily check for?
questions.a: Missing closing tags, invalid attributes, and structure violations
questions.d: The color contrast ratio for accessibility
questions.explanation: HTML Validators parse the DOM against the official specification to find syntax errors, improper nesting, and illegal attributes.

questions.question: According to accessibility standards, why is '<div> soup' (building a whole site using only <div> and <span> tags) considered harmful?
questions.b: It strips all semantic meaning from the page, making it impossible for screen readers to navigate via landmarks (like main, nav, header)
questions.c: It forces CSS to download slower
questions.d: It triggers infinite loops in JavaScript
questions.explanation: Without semantic tags (like <nav>, <main>, <button>), assistive technologies cannot provide structural context to visually impaired users.

questions.question: What are the four core principles of WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) represented by the acronym 'POUR'?
questions.explanation: POUR stands for Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust—the foundational pillars of WCAG standards.

questions.question: What does ARIA stand for in web accessibility?
questions.explanation: ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications, defining roles, states, and properties for assistive tech.

questions.question: What is the First Rule of ARIA use according to W3C guidelines?
questions.a: Add ARIA roles to every single HTML tag
questions.b: If you can use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, then do so instead of adding ARIA
questions.c: Never use native HTML elements if ARIA is available
questions.d: Only use ARIA on mobile devices
questions.explanation: Native semantic HTML elements (like <button>, <nav>) have built-in accessibility; ARIA should only supplement when native tags are insufficient.

questions.question: What does 'aria-label' do on an HTML element?
questions.b: Provides an explicit accessible string label for screen readers, overriding any internal text content
questions.explanation: aria-label supplies an accessible name string directly read by screen readers (e.g. on icon buttons like <button aria-label="Close">X</button>).

questions.question: What does 'aria-labelledby' do?
questions.a: References the ID of another element in the document whose text content serves as the accessible label for the current element
questions.b: Creates a sub-label in a form
questions.d: Links to an external copyright page
questions.explanation: aria-labelledby="headingId" computes the accessible name from the text of the referenced element(s).

questions.question: What does 'aria-describedby' do?
questions.a: Sets the author description meta tag
questions.b: References the ID of an element that provides detailed secondary descriptive text (such as help text or error messages)
questions.explanation: aria-describedby associates an input with auxiliary instructional or error text read after the label by screen readers.

questions.question: What does 'aria-live="polite"' do in dynamic web applications?
questions.a: Speaks text loudly over speakers immediately
questions.b: Instructs screen readers to announce dynamic content updates to this region when the user is idle, without interrupting active speech
questions.c: Politely asks user for camera permissions
questions.explanation: aria-live="polite" queues dynamic announcements to be spoken once the user finishes their current task/keystrokes.

questions.question: What does 'aria-live="assertive"' do?
questions.b: Instructs screen readers to immediately interrupt whatever is currently being spoken to announce critical high-priority updates (e.g. server error alerts)
questions.c: Forces the browser to focus the element
questions.explanation: aria-live="assertive" immediately interrupts current speech output for urgent or time-sensitive announcements.

questions.question: What is the effect of 'tabindex="0"' on a <div> element?
questions.a: Removes the element from tab order
questions.b: Places the element into the natural keyboard tab navigation order in sequence with surrounding interactive elements
questions.c: Makes the element the very first item focused when page loads
questions.d: Opens the element in a new browser tab
questions.explanation: tabindex="0" makes non-interactive elements focusable via keyboard Tab key in natural document source order.

questions.question: What is the effect of 'tabindex="-1"' on an element?
questions.a: The element cannot be focused at all
questions.b: The element is removed from keyboard sequential tab navigation, but can still be programmatically focused via JavaScript (element.focus())
questions.c: The element is focused in reverse order
questions.d: The element is hidden from screen readers
questions.explanation: tabindex="-1" enables programmatic focus via JS while excluding the element from keyboard Tab navigation.

questions.question: Why are positive tabindex values (e.g. tabindex="1", tabindex="5") strongly discouraged by accessibility standards?
questions.b: They override natural tab order, confusing keyboard users and creating frustrating, unpredictable navigation flows
questions.explanation: Positive tabindex creates an unnatural, hard-to-maintain focus order that disorients keyboard and screen reader users.

questions.question: What is a 'Skip Link' (Skip to Main Content link) in accessible web design?
questions.a: A link that skips commercial ads
questions.b: A hidden link at the very top of the page that allows keyboard and screen reader users to bypass repetitive header navigation and jump straight to main content
questions.c: A link that navigates to the next article
questions.d: A button that fast-forwards audio tracks
questions.explanation: Skip navigation links allow keyboard and screen reader users to jump past extensive header navigation directly to main content.

questions.question: What HTML entity represents an ampersand character (&)?
questions.explanation: & represents the literal ampersand symbol '&' in HTML source markup.

questions.question: What HTML entity represents a 'greater than' symbol (>)?
questions.explanation: > (Greater Than) displays the '>' character without confusing the HTML parser.

questions.question: What HTML entity represents the copyright symbol (©)?
questions.explanation: © produces the copyright symbol '©'.

questions.question: What HTML entity represents a standard registered trademark symbol (®)?
questions.explanation: ® renders the registered trademark symbol '®'.

questions.question: What does the WHATWG acronym stand for?
questions.a: Web Hosting and Technology Working Group
questions.b: Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group
questions.d: World HTML Accessibility Testing Working Group
questions.explanation: WHATWG stands for Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group, the organization maintaining the HTML Living Standard.

questions.question: What is an HTML 'Living Standard'?
questions.a: A standard that requires payment to read
questions.b: A continuously maintained and evolving standard without static version numbers (like HTML5.0, HTML6), continuously updated in response to web needs
questions.c: A standard for biological simulations in HTML
questions.d: A legacy archive maintained by CERN
questions.explanation: The HTML Living Standard continuously evolves and updates rather than publishing frozen major version increments.

questions.question: What is the minimum WCAG 2.1 Level AA color contrast ratio required for normal body text against its background?
questions.explanation: WCAG Level AA mandates a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text (and 3:1 for large text).

questions.question: Why should color NEVER be used as the sole visual means of conveying critical information (e.g. required form fields marked only in red)?
questions.a: Because red ink is more expensive to print
questions.b: Because color-blind users and screen reader users cannot perceive or distinguish information conveyed only through color differences
questions.c: Because CSS colors slow down mobile GPU rendering
questions.d: Because dark mode overrides all colors automatically
questions.explanation: WCAG requires that information conveyed with color also includes text labels, icons, or patterns so color-blind users can understand it.
